rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Newton's second law (ΣF = ma) applied through free-body diagrams solves every mechanics problem: elevators (apparent weight), Atwood's machine, connected bodies, inclined planes (smooth and rough), and objects in fluids. The key is correct isolation of the body and accurate force identification. Pseudo-forces allow analysis in non-inertial frames.

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Newton's second law (vector): ΣF = ma → ΣF_x = ma_x, ΣF_y = ma_y
Elevator apparent weight: N = m(g ± a) where + is upward acceleration, − is downward
Atwood's machine: a = (m₁ − m₂)g/(m₁ + m₂); T = 2m₁m₂g/(m₁ + m₂)

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Inertial Frame Requirement:** Newton's laws ($F=ma$) hold only in inertial reference frames. In accelerating (non-inertial) frames, a pseudo-force $-ma_{frame}$ must be added to the FBD to make the equations valid.  ·  **FBD Completeness:** The free-body diagram must include *all* forces acting ON the chosen body: weight, normal, friction, tension, applied forces. Forces exerted BY the body on other objects do NOT belong in its FBD.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Always draw the FBD BEFORE writing equations — a wrong diagram guarantees a wrong answer.  ·  Choose one axis along the direction of acceleration — this makes ma appear on only one axis.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Elevator: A 70 kg person stands on a scale in an elevator accelerating upward at 2 m/s². Scale reading = m(g + a) = 70(9.8 + 2) = 826 N (apparent mass ≈ 84.3 kg).  ·  Atwood: m₁ = 6 kg, m₂ = 4 kg. a = (6−4)×9.8/(6+4) = 1.96 m/s²; T = 2×6×4×9.8/10 = 47.04 N.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: ❌ 'The normal force is always mg.' ✅ N = mg only on a horizontal surface with no vertical acceleration. On a slope N = mg cos θ; in an accelerating elevator N = m(g ± a).  ·  ❌ 'Friction always opposes motion.' ✅ Friction opposes RELATIVE motion (or its tendency). Static friction can act in the direction of motion — e.g., the static friction on your feet pushes you forward when walking.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Draw free-body diagrams for 10 different mechanical scenarios and write the ΣF = ma equations.  ·  Solve 5 elevator problems computing apparent weight for upward, downward, and free-fall cases.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Elevator shortcut: apparent weight = m(g ± a) — just add or subtract ma from the real weight.  ·  Atwood shortcut: a = (m₁ − m₂)g/(m₁ + m₂) — the net driving force is the weight difference; total inertia is the total mass.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: A 60 kg woman stands on a scale in a lift moving upward at 3 m/s². What does the scale read? What if the lift cable breaks?  ·  Two masses 5 kg and 3 kg hang over a frictionless pulley. Find the acceleration and tension.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: The FBD carries marks — draw it clearly, label all forces, and show the coordinate axes.  ·  Elevator and Atwood problems appear almost every year — master both.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Newton's second law (ΣF = ma) is the master equation connecting forces to motion in mechanics.  ·  The free-body diagram (FBD) is the essential first step — it identifies all forces acting on a single body.  ·  Apparent weight changes with acceleration: N = m(g ± a) — the basis of weightlessness.  ·  Atwood's machine and connected bodies demonstrate how tension transmits force between bodies.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: The FBD method is universal: isolate → draw forces → choose axes → ΣF = ma → solve.  ·  The normal force adapts to the situation — it is NOT always mg.  ·  Tension in an accelerating string differs from the weight of the attached mass.  ·  Action-reaction pairs act on different bodies — never cancel in a single FBD.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Newton's second law (ΣF = ma) is the master equation of mechanics — it connects forces to motion.  ·  Every mechanics problem in the NEB exam can be solved by drawing a correct FBD and applying ΣF = ma.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: A block slides down a smooth 45° incline. Find the time to travel 4 m from rest.  ·  A 40 N force pushes two blocks (3 kg and 7 kg) on a smooth horizontal surface. Find the contact force between them.  ·  A 2 kg block rests on a 30° rough slope (μ = 0.4). Does it slide? If so, find the acceleration.

rows.label: More hints
rows.text: Inclined plane problems (smooth and rough) are standard — know the mg sin θ and mg cos θ decomposition.  ·  Connected-body problems test both system thinking (find a) and isolation thinking (find contact forces).

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: Incline: A 10 kg block on a 37° smooth slope — a = g sin 37° = 9.8 × 0.6 = 5.88 m/s² down the slope.  ·  Connected: F = 30 N pushes m₁ = 2 kg, m₂ = 3 kg, m₃ = 5 kg. a = 30/10 = 3 m/s²; contact force between m₁ and m₂ = (3+5)×3 = 24 N.

rows.label: MCQ drill
rows.text: A block of mass 5 kg rests on a smooth inclined plane at 30°. Its acceleration down the plane is: (g = 10 m/s²) → A  ·  A 60 kg person stands on a scale in an elevator moving downward at constant speed. The scale reads: → B

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **The problem-solving framework (the 'FBD method'):** (1) isolate the body, (2) draw ALL forces acting ON it (weight, normal, friction, tension, applied), (3) choose axes (one along acceleration), (4) write $ΣF = ma$ for each axis, (5) solve. Every single NEB numerical follows this pattern.  ·  **Elevator weight paradox:** in an accelerating upward elevator, the normal force $N = m(g + a)$ — you feel heavier. Accelerating downward: $N = m(g - a)$ — you feel lighter. Free fall ($a = g$): $N = 0$ (weightlessness). The weight $mg$ never changes; what changes is the apparent weight (the normal force).  ·  **Atwood's machine (two masses on a pulley):** acceleration $a = \frac{(m_1 - m_2)g}{m_1 + m_2}$; tension $T = \frac{2m_1 m_2 g}{m_1 + m_2}$. The string is massless and inextensible; the pulley is frictionless — if not, extra terms appear.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: On an inclined plane, weight decomposes into mg sin θ (along slope) and mg cos θ (into slope).  ·  Pseudo-forces are necessary for analyzing motion in non-inertial reference frames.  ·  Concept 1: Core definition of Application of Newton's laws

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **Friction Direction Logic:** Friction always opposes *relative motion or its tendency*. Static friction can act in the direction of motion (e.g., walking forward, car accelerating) — determine direction by asking 'which way would the surface slip without friction?'  ·  On a frictionless incline, all bodies slide at the same rate (independent of mass).  ·  Pseudo-forces are necessary in non-inertial frames.
